board_asks: the two direction rules (right-hand thumb rule for the field around a wire, Fleming's left-hand rule for the force on a wire), the properties of magnetic field lines, the field pattern of a solenoid compared with a bar magnet, and why a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force — plus the domestic-circuit safety questions (live / neutral / earth wire, fuse, earthing, overloading and short-circuit) and the AC-vs-DC contrast with the 50 Hz supply frequency. These are mostly 1-3 mark direction-and-reasoning questions, not numericals.

big_idea.tagline: A current makes a magnet; a magnet pushes a current.
big_idea.body: Every electric current wraps a magnetic field around itself, and a current-carrying wire placed in someone else's magnetic field feels a sideways push. Two hand rules capture the geometry: the right-hand thumb rule tells you which way the field curls around a wire, and Fleming's left-hand rule tells you which way the force pushes the wire. At home the same physics ends in a wall socket: 220 V alternating current at 50 Hz, carried by live, neutral and earth wires and protected by a fuse.

definitions.verbatim: The region surrounding a magnet, in which the force of the magnet can be detected, is said to have a magnetic field.
definitions.plain: the space around a magnet where its pull or push can be felt. It is a vector — it has both a direction and a magnitude.

definitions.verbatim: The lines along which the iron filings align themselves represent magnetic field lines.
definitions.plain: the imaginary curves that map a magnetic field. A tiny compass placed on a line points along it, so a field line is the path a free north pole would follow.

definitions.verbatim: Magnetic field is a quantity that has both direction and magnitude. The direction of the magnetic field is taken to be the direction in which a north pole of the compass needle moves inside it.
definitions.plain: point a compass anywhere in the field — the way its north pole turns is the field direction at that spot.

definitions.verbatim: Therefore it is taken by convention that the field lines emerge from north pole and merge at the south pole (note the arrows marked on the field lines in Fig. 12.4). Inside the magnet, the direction of field lines is from its south pole to its north pole. Thus the magnetic field lines are closed curves.
definitions.plain: outside the magnet field lines run N → S; inside they run S → N, so each line closes on itself. They never simply start or stop in mid-air.

definitions.term: Field strength and closeness of lines
definitions.verbatim: The relative strength of the magnetic field is shown by the degree of closeness of the field lines. The field is stronger, that is, the force acting on the pole of another magnet placed is greater where the field lines are crowded (see Fig. 12.4).
definitions.plain: crowded lines mean a strong field (near the poles); widely spaced lines mean a weak field.

definitions.verbatim: Imagine that you are holding a current-carrying straight conductor in your right hand such that the thumb points towards the direction of current. Then your fingers will wrap around the conductor in the direction of the field lines of the magnetic field, as shown in Fig. 12.7. This is known as the right-hand thumb rule.
definitions.plain: grip the wire with your right hand, thumb along the current; your curled fingers show which way the circular field lines go around the wire.

definitions.verbatim: A coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely in the shape of a cylinder is called a solenoid.
definitions.plain: a long, tightly wound cylindrical coil. Carrying current, it behaves like a bar magnet.

definitions.verbatim: The field lines inside the solenoid are in the form of parallel straight lines. This indicates that the magnetic field is the same at all points inside the solenoid. That is, the field is uniform inside the solenoid.
definitions.plain: deep inside the coil the field is the same everywhere — same strength and direction (a uniform field).

definitions.verbatim: A strong magnetic field produced inside a solenoid can be used to magnetise a piece of magnetic material, like soft iron, when placed inside the coil (Fig. 12.11). The magnet so formed is called an electromagnet.
definitions.plain: put a soft-iron core inside a current-carrying solenoid and it becomes a strong magnet — an electromagnet — only while the current flows.

definitions.verbatim: According to this rule, stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of your left hand such that they are mutually perpendicular (Fig. 12.13). If the first finger points in the direction of magnetic field and the second finger in the direction of current, then the thumb will point in the direction of motion or the force acting on the conductor.
definitions.plain: left hand, three fingers at right angles: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force). It gives the direction of the push on the wire.

definitions.verbatim: No two field-lines are found to cross each other. If they did, it would mean that at the point of intersection, the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.
The field lines about the wire consist of a series of concentric circles whose direction is given by the right-hand rule.

Experiments have shown that the displacement of the rod is largest (or the magnitude of the force is the highest) when the direction of current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field.

One of the wires in this supply, usually with red insulation cover, is called live wire (or positive). Another wire, with black insulation, is called neutral wire (or negative). In our country, the potential difference between the two is 220 V.
definitions.plain: the two wires that actually power an appliance: red = live, black = neutral, 220 V between them. Every appliance is connected across these two.

definitions.verbatim: The earth wire, which has insulation of green colour, is usually connected to a metal plate deep in the earth near the house. This is used as a safety measure, especially for those appliances that have a metallic body, for example, electric press, toaster, table fan, refrigerator, etc.
definitions.plain: the green third wire. It joins the metal body of an appliance to the earth, giving any leaked current a low-resistance path so the body stays at earth potential and the user is not shocked.

definitions.verbatim: Overloading can occur when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact. (This occurs when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance.) In such a situation, the current in the circuit abruptly increases. This is called short-circuiting.
definitions.plain: a short circuit is live touching neutral — the current jumps. Overloading also happens when the supply voltage spikes or too many appliances hang off one socket.

definitions.verbatim: The use of an electric fuse prevents the electric circuit and the appliance from a possible damage by stopping the flow of unduly high electric current. The Joule heating that takes place in the fuse melts it to break the electric circuit.
In order that each appliance has equal potential difference, they are connected parallel to each other.
In our houses we receive AC electric power of 220 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.

concepts.title: Magnetic field lines and their properties
concepts.body: Field lines picture the field: they run from N to S outside a magnet and close inside it, they are crowded where the field is strong, and no two ever cross. These four properties are the standard short-answer.
concepts.tested: 2–3 mark "list the properties of magnetic field lines" / "why don't two field lines cross?"

concepts.title: Magnetic field due to a straight current-carrying conductor
concepts.body: A straight wire is surrounded by concentric circular field lines. Their direction is found by the right-hand thumb rule; the field grows with the current ($B \propto I$) and weakens with distance ($B \propto 1/r$).
concepts.tested: 2-mark "find the direction of the field" using the right-hand thumb rule

concepts.title: Field due to a circular loop and a coil
concepts.body: Bend the wire into a loop and every part of it pushes the field the same way through the centre, so the field there is strong and nearly straight. A coil of $n$ turns gives $n$ times the field of a single turn, because each turn adds up.
concepts.tested: 2-mark reasoning "why is the field stronger at the centre of a coil?"

concepts.title: Solenoid and the electromagnet
concepts.body: A current-carrying solenoid has a field pattern identical to a bar magnet — one end a north pole, the other a south pole — and a uniform field inside. A soft-iron core inside it becomes a strong electromagnet.
concepts.tested: 3-mark "compare the field of a solenoid with a bar magnet" / electromagnet

concepts.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor
concepts.body: A wire carrying current in a magnetic field feels a force perpendicular to both. The force is largest when the current is at right angles to the field, and it reverses if either the current or the field is reversed. Its direction is read off Fleming's left-hand rule.
concepts.tested: 2–3 mark "state the rule / find the direction of the force"

concepts.title: Direct current and alternating current
concepts.body: A cell or battery drives a direct current (DC) — it flows in one direction only. The mains supply is an alternating current (AC) that reverses its direction periodically; in India it is 220 V at a frequency of 50 Hz, so the current completes 50 cycles every second (it changes direction every 1/100 s). The board-listed advantage of AC over DC: electric power can be transmitted over long distances without much loss of energy, which is why the grid delivers AC to homes.
concepts.tested: 1-mark recall (frequency of AC in India) · 2-mark distinguish AC from DC / state one advantage of AC over DC

source.note: 220 V / 50 Hz from the chapter Summary p.206; the DC-vs-AC contrast and the advantage of AC are the CBSE 2026-27 syllabus items 'Direct current. Alternating current: frequency of AC. Advantage of AC over DC' (Science p.6) — those sentences sit in the NCERT reference material CBSE encloses, not in the 2026-27 chapter body

concepts.title: Domestic electric circuits — live, neutral, earth, fuse
concepts.body: Mains power enters through a main fuse and the meter, then splits into separate circuits — a 15 A circuit for high-power appliances (geysers, air coolers) and a 5 A circuit for bulbs and fans. Each appliance sits in parallel across the live (red) and neutral (black) wires, so every one gets the full 220 V and has its own switch. The green earth wire ties metal bodies to the earth so a leak cannot shock the user. A fuse melts by Joule heating when the current rises too high — through short-circuiting (live touching neutral), a voltage surge, or too many appliances on one socket (overloading).
concepts.tested: 2–3 mark 'function of the earth wire / why are appliances connected in parallel / when does a short circuit occur' (NCERT Exercise Q8, Q9) · 1-mark true/false on wire colours (Exercise Q6)

source.note: Section 12.4 Domestic Electric Circuits, p.204-205 and Fig. 12.15

examples.shape: Right-hand thumb rule — field near a power line
examples.problem_verbatim: A current through a horizontal power line flows in east to west direction. What is the direction of magnetic field at a point directly below it and at a point directly above it?

solution_steps.text: The current is along the wire, from east to west.
Point the right thumb from east to west (along the current); the curled fingers give the field, which lies in a plane perpendicular to the wire.

The magnetic field turns clockwise when viewed from the east end and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end — so at the point below the wire and the point above it, the field points in opposite directions.

examples.mark_logic: 1 mark for correctly applying the right-hand thumb rule, 1 mark for the clockwise/anti-clockwise sense (equivalently, that the field is oppositely directed below and above the wire).

examples.shape: Fleming's left-hand rule — force on a moving electron
examples.problem_verbatim: An electron enters a magnetic field at right angles to it, as shown in Fig. 12.14. The direction of force acting on the electron will be (a) to the right. (b) to the left. (c) out of the page. (d) into the page.

solution_steps.text: Conventional current is taken opposite to the electron's direction of motion.
First finger along the field and second finger along the (conventional) current make the thumb — the force — point into the page. Answer: option (d).

examples.mark_logic: 1 mark for option (d) with the Fleming's left-hand-rule justification — the key trap is remembering that conventional current is opposite to the electron's motion.

strategies.text: Right hand — thumb along the current, curled fingers give the circular field. Reverse the current and the field reverses.
Fleming's LEFT hand — First finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion/force. Don't reach for the right hand here.
Say it out loud: its field is identical to a bar magnet, uniform inside, one end N and one end S; a soft-iron core makes an electromagnet.
Four marks-earners: N→S outside / closed curves / crowded = strong / never cross.

Name the wire by colour and job — red live, black neutral, green earth — then give the safety reason: earthing for metal bodies, fuse (melts by Joule heating) against overloading and short-circuit, appliances in parallel so each gets 220 V.
DC flows one way (cells, batteries); AC reverses periodically — 220 V, 50 Hz in India. Advantage of AC: long-distance transmission without much loss of energy.

pitfalls.text: ✗ Swapping the two rules — use the RIGHT hand for the field around a wire, the LEFT hand for the force on a wire.
✗ In the electron problem, forgetting that conventional current is opposite to the electron's motion — it flips the force direction.
✗ Calling field lines open — they are closed curves (S→N inside the magnet).
✗ Drawing two field lines that cross — impossible, since a compass can't point two ways at once.
✗ Calling the green wire the live wire — NCERT's own true/false item (Exercise Q6) sets this trap. Red is live, black neutral, green earth.

third_tab_content.intro: This chapter is about DIRECTIONS, not formulas. Two hand rules do almost all the work — keep them straight, and note how the field's size changes with current and distance. The last two blocks are the household end: wire colours, the fuse, and AC versus DC.

blocks.heading: Right-hand thumb rule — direction of the field around a straight wire
items: Grip the wire with your right hand.
Point the thumb along the direction of the current.
The curled fingers give the direction of the circular field lines.
Reverse the current and the field direction reverses.

blocks.heading: Fleming's left-hand rule — direction of the force on the wire

rows.text: points along the Motion / force on the conductor.
Outside the magnet lines run north to south; inside, south to north — so they are closed curves.
No two field lines ever cross (a compass cannot point two ways).
Crowded lines = strong field; widely spaced lines = weak field.
Farther from the wire → weaker field ($B \propto 1/r$).
A coil of $n$ turns gives $n$ times the field of one turn.

blocks.heading: Domestic circuit — wire colours and safety

rows.text: Live wire — 220 V with respect to the neutral.
Earth wire — ties metallic bodies to the earth so leaked current cannot shock the user.
Melts by Joule heating on overloading or a short circuit, breaking the circuit.
Appliances are connected in parallel — each gets the full potential difference and its own switch.
Separate circuits for high-power appliances (geysers, coolers) and for bulbs and fans.

blocks.heading: Direct current vs alternating current
items: DC (cells, batteries) flows in one direction only.
AC reverses its direction periodically — India's supply is 220 V at 50 Hz.
Advantage of AC over DC: it can be transmitted over long distances without much loss of energy.

fig_domestic_circuit_1215.caption: A common domestic circuit — live (red) and neutral (black) come from the mains through the Electricity Board's fuse, the electricity meter and the distribution box (main switch plus a fuse for each circuit); every socket sits across the 220 V live–neutral pair, in parallel; the earth wire (green) runs to the earth pin of each socket.
fig_domestic_circuit_1215.legend: Follow the red wire left to right: fuse → meter → distribution box → top rail. Each socket hangs between the red and black rails (parallel, so each gets the full 220 V); the green wire crosses the live rail without joining it (the small jump) and ends on the socket's earth pin.
